title: Looking back: the stories
hookLine: Genesis, Exodus, the prophets and the kings
tomorrow: Hillel lit one candle the first night, Shammai eight. who was right?

lines: WHY THE CANDLES? WHY THE CHAIR?
cards: A kid at the dinner table asks why. Why the candles, why the extra chair, why we don't do that on Saturday. The quick reply is: because those are the rules.
Deuteronomy writes out a stranger script. A child asks, in the JPS translation: "What mean the testimonies, and the statutes, and the ordinances?" That's a question about rules.
And the answer the Torah gives the parent is not a rule at all. It starts: "We were Pharaoh's bondmen in Egypt." A question about law, answered with a story.

teach.h: THE RULES LIVE INSIDE THE STORY.
teach.b: Here's one way to solve it. The rules only make sense from inside the story. Rest on the seventh day means something different to people who remember being slaves who never rested.
Welcome the stranger lands differently when you were once strangers yourselves. So the Torah hands the parent a story first and lets the laws follow it home.

A parent could say it at dinner in one line: we do this because of a story, and here it is. And a detail worth repeating at dinner: the Passover Haggadah puts this very question in the mouth of the wise child.

teach.h: THE WISE CHILD GETS A STORY.
teach.b: The wise one is the one who asks about the rules, and gets the story. Now look back over the road.
Genesis: a family that keeps breaking and mending, brothers who sell a brother and bow to him years later.
Exodus: a sea that opens, a mountain wrapped in smoke. The prophets: a still small voice after the wind and the fire. The kings: David with a harp, and David caught by a parable he didn't see coming.
Stories don't wear out the way rules can. You can tell them to a small child and to yourself in old age, and they answer different questions each time.

how: At the Passover seder, Jewish families answer the children's questions with the Exodus story, reading from the Haggadah, which gives Deuteronomy 6:20's question to the wise child.

games.q: your nephew asks why his family won't drive to the mall on Saturday. he's six. you've got one minute. how do you start?
o: "once, a long time ago, our people were slaves who never got a day off…"
"because there are rules about Saturday, and we follow the rules."
"you'll understand when you're older and can read it yourself."
games.why: Deuteronomy's script answers a child's question about laws with the story first. the rule makes sense from inside it.

practice: Pick the story from this path you'd tell first if a child asked you why. Tell it out loud, in your own words, in about the time the bell gives you: who was there, what went wrong, what happened next. Don't explain it at the end.
Let the story do the work. If someone's in the room with you, tell it to them instead.

wordCard.voice: Looking back: the stories. Genesis, Exodus, the prophets and the kings, told so that the rules have somewhere to live, and told again.
